newsitem.title: GERMANY: Focus-German AMB unfazed by larger rival.
newsitem.headline: Focus-German AMB unfazed by larger rival.

text.p: Aachener und Muenchener Beteiligungs-AG (AMB) said on Wednesday it was looking toward a steady future amid lower costs despite being knocked from the No. 2 spot in German insurance by the newly-formed Ergo group.
Wolfgang Kaske, chairman of the company now demoted to third place on the market, told a news conference the surprise merger that created Ergo in early July was "an intelligent idea."
"But we won't let Ergo scare us," he added.

Ergo will be formed from a fusion of reinsurer Muenchener Rueckversicherungs AG's primary insurance units with Victoria Holding AG, a composite insurer that had been widely expected to be snapped up from abroad.

The new company will have total premium income of some 21 billion marks ($11.7 billion) and more than 14 million customers, making it Germany's second ranked insurer after Allianz AG, the industry giant with annual 1996 premiums of 75 billion marks.
AMB is focusing on an internal restructuring, which Kaske said would yield cost savings of 400 million marks a year in the medium-term.

The company aims to tighten its operations, has settled contracts to give it more control of major units and has decided to merge reinsurer AMB Konzernrueckverischerungs AG into the main AMB Holding group.
The insurer is certain to at least hold its profits at year-ago levels this year despite ongoing weakness on the non-life sales side, Kaske said.

A whole series of cost-cuts were already secured for the current year, leading to savings of some 90 million marks. Plans to centralise its computer systems would alone lead to savings of some 45 million marks.

AMB reported group 1996 net profit of 343.3 million marks , while premiums rose 5.4 percent to 17.1 billion marks at parent level. Sales reached 20 billion marks at group level, counting mortgage unit Badenia Bausparkasse.
The company acknowledged that sales growth would be limited to around four percent this year.

In the first five months, AMB posted a premium rise of 5.4 percent to 7.8 billion marks. But damage and accident insurance fell by 0.1 percent in the period, while life insurance new business grew above average by 3.5 percent.

Kaske, who is due to retire this year and be succeeded by chairman-designate Hans Jaeger, said AMB would pay an unchanged dividend in 1997. In 1996, the dividend payout was increased to 16 marks per share from 15 marks.

As talk circulates of inevitable consolidation in the overcrowded German financial services industry, particularly given tougher European competition, Kaske said he was confident AMB was not at any immediate risk of a takeover bid.
He said AGF, AMB's French main shareholder, was very happy with its ownership level and had pledged not to make any changes until the end of 1999.
AGF owns 33.5 percent of AMB's shares and controls 27.5 percent of its voting rights.
The remaining AMB shareholders are Dresdner Bank AG with 14.7 percent, Munich Re with 8.6 percent and Allianz AG with five percent, Kaske said.
Some 38.2 percent of the share capital was held by small shareholders.
--Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525
($ = 1.791 German Marks)
